findings.content: The documentation says the fallback chain tries OSC52 first, but copy_to_clipboard only attempts OSC52 when stdout is a TTY and SSH_CONNECTION or SSH_TTY is present. In non-SSH local terminals the first attempted method is arboard, so the module-level docs overstate the actual order.

`Drop` writes lifecycle messages to stdout, which can pollute command output and break CLI consumers that parse stdout. Cleanup code should avoid normal stdout; use stderr/debug logging or stay silent.

If URL extraction times out after spawning cloudflared, `start` returns an error without killing or waiting on the child process. Dropping `std::process::Child` does not terminate the process, so failed login attempts can leave orphaned tunnel processes running.

Linux clipboard helper discovery only tries to execute each helper with `--version` (and then the same binary with `-v`), so a helper that exists but does not support those flags or exits non-zero will be treated as unavailable even though the subsequent stdin-based invocation would work. That makes clipboard copy fail unnecessarily in otherwise valid CLI environments. Prefer PATH lookup that does not execute the helper with tool-specific flags, or just attempt `try_command_with_stdin` and rely on spawn failure for missing commands.

The public API documentation for `start` says it starts a cloudflared tunnel and returns an instance, but it omits an important ownership side effect: the spawned tunnel is automatically killed when the returned `CloudflaredTunnel` is dropped. Callers reading the docs could accidentally drop the value immediately after reading `public_url()` and terminate the OAuth tunnel before the callback completes. Documenting this RAII behavior makes the lifecycle contract accurate.

The logout command documentation says it removes authentication, but the implementation only deletes the legacy bot token key and profile. User tokens saved under the separate `team_id:user_id:user` key and the saved OAuth client secret are left behind, so the documented behavior is misleading and stale credentials remain after logout.

`auth logout` only deletes the bot token key. Profiles created by the OAuth flow also store a user token at `team_id:user_id:user` and the OAuth client secret at `oauth-client-secret:<profile>`, so logout leaves usable credentials behind despite reporting that authentication was removed.

The extended login function documents cloudflared/ngrok tunnel support, but `use_cloudflared == false` falls back to a localhost redirect instead of starting an ngrok tunnel. Because the CLI accepts `--ngrok`, users can request ngrok and silently get a non-public callback URL, breaking the advertised command contract.

derive_key ignores KdfParams.memory_cost, time_cost, and parallelism and always uses Argon2::default(), even though those parameters are serialized with exported files. Any export/import using non-default KDF metadata will not derive the documented key and the saved parameters become misleading.

`KdfParams` exposes `memory_cost`, `time_cost`, and `parallelism`, and the comment says these are Argon2id KDF parameters, but `derive_key` ignores all three by constructing `Argon2::default()`. Exported payloads can therefore document non-default KDF parameters that are not actually used for key derivation, making the crypto metadata misleading and preventing parameter changes from taking effect.

`fs::write` creates or truncates the export file before permissions are tightened to 0600, so on Unix a new backup can briefly exist with process-umask permissions (for example 0644) even though it contains encrypted Slack tokens. Create the file with mode 0600 from the start and write through that handle.

When `--force` overwrites a conflicting profile, the old profile is removed from the config but its stored credentials are left behind. Because tokens are keyed by the old team/user pair and OAuth client secrets by profile name, forced imports can leave stale Slack credentials in the token store after the CLI reports an overwrite.

findings.content: The generated YAML is rejected unless it starts directly with `_metadata:` or `"_metadata":`. YAML serializers may prepend a document marker (`---`) while still producing valid YAML, so this check can turn valid output into a CLI failure. Validate by parsing the YAML back or remove the serialization-order assertion.

`profile_name` is embedded directly into the manifest display name, description, and bot display name without validation. A profile name containing newlines or characters unsupported by Slack bot display names can generate a manifest that the CLI writes/copies successfully but Slack rejects, breaking the manifest-first flow. Validate or sanitize profile names before building manifest fields.

The test name and setup imply this covers a cloudflared-specific manifest, but the test passes a localhost redirect URI and only asserts generic scope/redirect behavior. This documentation-style test name is misleading and duplicates the non-tunnel behavior, so future readers may believe cloudflared redirect handling is verified here when it is not.

This test has the same docs-accuracy issue as the cloudflared case: the name says ngrok, but the input is localhost and the assertions do not exercise an ngrok URL. That makes the test read as tunnel-specific documentation while only verifying generic redirect serialization.

The documentation states this extracts the public URL from ngrok output, but the implementation only accepts ngrok-free.app domains. Ngrok also emits other public hostnames depending on account/reserved domains, so the doc overstates supported ngrok output and can mislead callers when valid HTTPS tunnel URLs are ignored.

After sending the first public URL, both output-reader threads break and stop draining ngrok's stdout/stderr. If ngrok continues writing logs while the tunnel is active, the child process can block on a full pipe and the OAuth flow may hang. Keep reading after the URL is sent, as the cloudflared tunnel implementation does.

If URL extraction times out, start() returns an error while leaving the spawned ngrok process running. That leaks a background tunnel and can keep the local port/process alive after a failed login attempt. Kill and wait for the child before returning the timeout error.

`conv_list` follows `next_cursor` until Slack stops returning one, but it has no cycle guard or maximum page bound. If Slack or a proxy repeatedly returns the same non-empty cursor, this CLI command can loop indefinitely and keep issuing API requests. Track seen cursors and fail on repeats to preserve the CLI contract of terminating predictably.

The documentation says conv_list returns an Ok(ApiResponse) with all pages aggregated, but the implementation uses ApiClient::call_method, which returns Err on any Slack response with ok=false. As a result, Slack API errors are not returned as Ok(ApiResponse) with ok=false/error populated, making the Returns documentation inaccurate for error responses.

Wildcard name filters are documented as glob-style matching, but the wildcard branch is case-sensitive while non-wildcard matching is case-insensitive. This makes `--filter=name:test*` fail to match channels such as `TEST-channel`, even though `--filter=name:test` would match them. Normalize both pattern and text before wildcard matching, or document wildcard filters as case-sensitive.

Non-JSON formats silently turn Slack API errors into empty successful output. If conversations.list returns ok=false without a channels array, the jsonl/table/tsv branches return an empty string, so callers print nothing and still return Ok, which breaks the CLI contract for scripts because authentication/scope failures are indistinguishable from an empty result set.

findings.content: The query parser splits each pair on every '=' and only keeps the first two pieces. Slack OAuth callback values are URL-encoded, but malformed or future parameters containing an unescaped '=' will be silently truncated. Use split_once so only the first separator divides key and value, matching query-string semantics.

The custom percent decoder pushes decoded bytes as individual chars, which corrupts non-ASCII UTF-8 sequences such as %E3%81%82 into mojibake. OAuth state/code are generally ASCII, but error messages and arbitrary query values can be UTF-8; percent decoding should collect bytes and validate UTF-8.

The module documentation says token storage uses the OS keyring, but the exported token store implementation currently creates a file-backed store via `FileTokenStore::new()`, which stores tokens in a JSON file with restricted permissions. This stale documentation can mislead users and reviewers about where Slack tokens are persisted and what security boundary protects them.

The migration helper documents the copy fallback as keeping the old file, but after a successful `fs::rename` the legacy file is removed. This makes the function behavior ambiguous for callers/tests reading the doc comment; clarify that the old file is kept only when the copy fallback is used.

`set` mutates the in-memory token map before persisting it. If `save_tokens()` fails (for example due to a permission error, full disk, or the backing file being replaced by an unwritable path), the method returns an error but the current `FileTokenStore` instance now serves the unsaved token from memory. That can make later auth operations appear to have succeeded until the process restarts, while the credential was never durably stored. Persist a cloned updated map first, or roll back the insertion on save failure so the in-memory state matches the returned error.

`delete` removes the token from memory before persisting the file. If `save_tokens()` fails, the method returns an error but this process has already forgotten the token, while the old token may still be present on disk. That creates inconsistent behavior between the running process and the next invocation. Restore the removed token when persistence fails, or write the updated contents atomically before committing the in-memory deletion.

The FileTokenStore documentation says the default path is always `~/.local/share/slack-rs/tokens.json`, but `default_path()` first honors `SLACK_RS_TOKENS_PATH` and then absolute `XDG_DATA_HOME`. This can mislead callers about where credentials are stored by default on systems with XDG_DATA_HOME set.

`FromStr` accepts values such as `" bot"` or `"user\n"` as invalid because it lowercases without trimming. For CLI input this makes otherwise normal whitespace-padded values fail, while the rest of the CLI commonly treats environment/config strings with trimming. Trim before matching, but keep the original value in the error for diagnostics.

`list_names` returns `HashMap` keys in iteration order, so `slack auth list` can print profiles in a nondeterministic order across runs. For a CLI command, stable ordering avoids flaky snapshots/scripts and makes output predictable.

The doc comment says local installs go to ./.agents when global is false, but the implementation resolves this relative to std::env::current_dir(), not necessarily the package/project root. If the CLI is invoked from a subdirectory, the skill will be installed under that subdirectory's .agents, so the documentation overstates the behavior and can mislead callers.
